title: Antarctic Circle: The Southern Line of Night
description: Explore the Antarctic Circle — the latitude of the southern polar night and midnight sun, its research stations and drifting position. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the Antarctic Circle sits at 66.5633°S and runs about 15,900 km around the continent's coast — almost entirely over ocean and ice that no road will ever cross.
quick_answer: The Antarctic Circle is the line at 66.5633 degrees south latitude where the Sun can stay up for 24 hours at the December solstice — and vanish for 24 hours at the June one. This page maps the circle and explains polar day and night down south.

Unlike its northern twin (eight countries, many towns), the Antarctic Circle crosses no country and almost no land communities — its ~15,900 km run is ocean, ice shelf and the Antarctic Peninsula's tip.
The circle creeps as Earth's tilt changes — roughly 15 metres a year, currently drifting southward in latitude terms as the tilt decreases and the polar-night zone shrinks slightly.

Why is Antarctica colder than the Arctic?
It is a high, ice-covered continent (the pole sits ~2,800 m up on ice) versus the Arctic's sea-level ocean — altitude and land ice win the cold contest.
The Antarctic Treaty system (1961) administers the continent for science; territorial claims are held in abeyance rather than settled.
Several species breed on the Peninsula and coasts around the circle — Adélies and gentoos among them; emperors breed further south on sea ice.
Is the circle visible from space as a line?
No more than any latitude — it is geometry, not geography. What satellites see is the day/night terminator respecting it at the solstices.
The Antarctic Convergence is a biological ocean boundary where cold southern water sinks — a wavy natural front, unrelated to the geometric circle but often confused with it.
